title: Office days or home days?
scenario: You chair a short team meeting. Dana and Tomas disagree about the new working pattern and are talking past each other. Help them understand each other's views and move towards a decision.

lines.t: On home days I finish more in a morning than I do in a whole day here. Nobody walks up to my desk every ten minutes.
But that is exactly the point. Our new starters learn by overhearing and asking quick questions. If everybody works from home, they lose that.
Then let them book a call. We do not need to sit in a room just to be available. Anyway, Tomas just likes an audience.
That is unfair. I am worried about the juniors, not about myself. And a call is not the same as a quick question across the desk.
Fine. But the coffee in this office is terrible, and the commute costs me two hours a day.
I am not saying everyone must come in five days. I just want us to be in at the same time sometimes.

task.audience: two colleagues who disagree in a meeting
task.prompt: Speak to Dana and Tomas (80–130 words). Show that you understand each view, name what they share, and suggest a practical way forward.

points.idea: Dana needs quiet days to concentrate.
Tomas worries that new starters learn less without informal contact.
Both want the team to work well and do not want five office days.
Try shared office days as a trial.

leave_out.idea: The remark about Tomas liking an audience.

model: Thank you both. Let me check I've understood. Dana, you get your best work done on home days because nobody interrupts you, so you need that time to focus. Tomas, you're worried that new starters will learn less if nobody is around to ask quick questions. I think you both want the same thing: a team that works well, and neither of you is asking for five days in the office. So how about a trial? We could agree on two shared office days, keep the other days flexible, and look at how it works after a month. Would that be acceptable to you both?
useful: I think you both want the same thing: …
Would that be acceptable to you both?
tips: Before you propose anything, describe each person's underlying need (focus, learning), not their position (home vs office). Needs overlap more than positions.
Leave out remarks about people ("just likes an audience") and respond only to the reasons. This keeps the discussion on the problem.
explain: The facilitator names Dana's need, Tomas's worry, what they share, and a small reversible trial. Repeating the personal jibe or the coffee complaint would add heat without helping.
